en.contentMarkdown:
# The Theia Collision: The Story of the Moon's Birth

Before life existed, before the oceans formed, even before the Moon lit the night sky, Earth was born from extraordinary cosmic chaos. This article takes you deep into the great events that shaped our planet's foundation, the violent processes that unfolded billions of years ago, and the journey from stardust to the world we inhabit today.

The giant-impact hypothesis, sometimes called the Theia Impact, is an astrogeology hypothesis for the formation of the Moon first proposed in 1946 by Canadian geologist Reginald Daly. The hypothesis suggests that the Proto-Earth collided with a Mars-sized co-orbital protoplanet likely from the L4 or L5 Lagrange points of the Earth's orbit approximately 4.5 billion years ago in the early Hadean eon (about 20 to 100 million years after the Solar System formed), and some of the ejected debris from the impact event later re-accreted to form the Moon. The impactor planet is sometimes called Theia, named after the mythical Greek Titan who was the mother of Selene, the goddess of the Moon.

Analysis of lunar rocks published in a 2016 report suggests that the impact might have been a direct hit, causing a fragmentation and thorough mixing of both parent bodies.

The giant-impact hypothesis is currently the favored hypothesis for lunar formation among astronomers. Evidence that supports this hypothesis includes:

The Moon's orbit has a similar orientation to Earth's rotation, both of which are at a similar angle to the ecliptic plane of the Solar System.

The stable isotope ratios of lunar and terrestrial rock are identical, implying a common origin.

The Earth–Moon system contains an anomalously high angular momentum, meaning the momentum contained in Earth's rotation, the Moon's rotation and the Moon's orbit around Earth is significantly higher than those of the other terrestrial planets. A giant impact could supply this excess momentum.

Moon samples indicate that the Moon was once molten to a substantial, but unknown, depth. This may have required much more energy than predicted to have been available from the accretion of a celestial body of the Moon's size and mass. An extremely energetic process, such as a giant impact, could provide this energy.

The Moon has a relatively small iron core, which gives it a much lower density than Earth. Computer models of a giant impact of a Mars-sized body with Earth indicate the impactor's core would likely penetrate deep into Earth and fuse with its own core. If this occurred, it would leave the Moon, which was formed from coalesced ejectae of lighter crustal and mantle fragments that went far enough beyond the Roche limit and thus were not pulled back by Earth's gravity to re-fuse with Earth, with less remaining metallic iron than other planetary bodies.

The Moon is depleted in volatile substances compared to Earth. Vaporizing at comparably lower temperatures, they could be lost in a high-energy event, with the Moon's smaller gravity unable to recapture them while Earth did.

There is evidence in other star systems of similar collisions, resulting in debris discs.

Giant collisions are consistent with the leading theory of the formation of the Solar System.

However, several questions remain concerning the best current models of the giant-impact hypothesis. The energy of such a giant impact is predicted to have heated Earth to produce a global magma ocean, and evidence of the resultant planetary differentiation of the heavier material sinking into Earth's mantle has been documented. However, there is no self-consistent model that starts with the giant-impact event and follows the evolution of the debris into a single moon.

![The Theia Collision: The Story of the Moon's Birth](/images/topics/sejarah-alt.svg)
*Gambar: The Theia Collision: The Story of the Moon's Birth*

## History

In 1898, George Darwin made the suggestion that Earth and the Moon were once a single body. Darwin's hypothesis was that a molten Moon had been spun from Earth because of centrifugal forces, and this became the dominant academic explanation. Using Newtonian mechanics, he calculated that the Moon had orbited much more closely in the past and was drifting away from Earth. This drifting was later confirmed by American and Soviet experiments, using laser ranging targets placed on the Moon.

Nonetheless, Darwin's calculations could not resolve the mechanics required to trace the Moon back to the surface of Earth. In 1946, Reginald Aldworth Daly of Harvard University challenged Darwin's explanation, adjusting it to postulate that the creation of the Moon was caused by an impact rather than centrifugal forces. Little attention was paid to Professor Daly's challenge until a conference on satellites in 1974, during which the idea was reintroduced and later published and discussed in Icarus in 1975 by William K. Hartmann and Donald R. Davis. Their models suggested that, at the end of the planet formation period, several satellite-sized bodies had formed that could collide with the planets or be captured. They proposed that one of these objects might have collided with Earth, ejecting refractory, volatile-poor dust that could coalesce to form the Moon. This collision could potentially explain the unique geological and geochemical properties of the Moon.

A similar approach was taken by Canadian astronomer Alastair G. W. Cameron and American astronomer William R. Ward, who suggested that the Moon was formed by the tangential impact upon Earth of a body the size of Mars. It is hypothesized that most of the outer silicates of the colliding body would be vaporized, whereas a metallic core would not. Hence, most of the collisional material sent into orbit would consist of silicates, leaving the coalescing Moon deficient in iron. The more volatile materials that were emitted during the collision probably would escape the Solar System, whereas silicates would tend to coalesce.

Eighteen months prior to an October 1984 conference on lunar origins, William K. Hartmann, Roger Phillips, and Jeff Taylor challenged fellow lunar scientists: "You have eighteen months. Go back to your Apollo data, go back to your computer, and do whatever you have to, but make up your mind. Don't come to our conference unless you have something to say about the Moon's birth." At the 1984 conference at Kona, Hawaii, the giant-impact hypothesis emerged as the most favored hypothesis.

Before the conference, there were partisans of the three "traditional" theories, plus a few people who were starting to take the giant impact seriously, and there was a huge apathetic middle who didn't think the debate would ever be resolved. Afterward, there were essentially only two groups: the giant impact camp and the agnostics.

## Theia

The name of the hypothesised protoplanet is derived from the mythical Greek titan Theia , who gave birth to the Moon goddess Selene. This designation was proposed initially by the English geochemist Alex N. Halliday in 2000 and has become accepted in the scientific community. According to modern theories of planet formation, Theia was part of a population of Mars-sized bodies that existed in the Solar System 4.5 billion years ago. Theia is hypothesized to have orbited in the L4 or L5 configuration presented by the Earth–Sun system, where it would tend to remain. One of the attractive features of the giant-impact hypothesis is that the formation of the Moon and Earth align; during the course of its formation, Earth is thought to have experienced dozens of collisions with planet-sized bodies. The Moon-forming collision would have been only one such "giant impact" but certainly the last significant impactor event. The Late Heavy Bombardment by much smaller asteroids may have occurred later – approximately 3.9 billion years ago.

## Basic model

Astronomers think the collision between Earth and Theia happened at about 4.4 to 4.45 billion years ago (bya); about 0.1 billion years after the Solar System began to form. In astronomical terms, the impact would have been of moderate velocity. Theia is thought to have struck Earth at an oblique angle when Earth was nearly fully formed. Computer simulations of this "late-impact" scenario suggest an initial impactor velocity below 4 kilometres per second (2.5 mi/s) at "infinity" (far enough that gravitational attraction is not a factor), increasing as it approached to over 9.3 km/s (5.8 mi/s) at impact, and an impact angle of about 45°. However, oxygen isotope abundance in lunar rock suggests "vigorous mixing" of Theia and Earth, indicating a steep impact angle. Theia's iron core would have sunk into the young Earth's core, and most of Theia's mantle accreted onto Earth's mantle. However, a significant portion of the mantle material from both Theia and Earth would have been ejected into orbit around Earth (if ejected with velocities between orbital velocity and escape velocity) or into individual orbits around the Sun (if ejected at higher velocities).

Modelling has hypothesised that material in orbit around Earth may have accreted to form the Moon in three consecutive phases, accreting first from the bodies initially present outside Earth's Roche limit, which acted to confine the inner disk material within the Roche limit. The inner disk slowly and viscously spread back out to Earth's Roche limit, pushing along outer bodies via resonant interactions. After several tens of years, the disk spread beyond the Roche limit, and started producing new objects that continued the growth of the Moon, until the inner disk was depleted in mass after several hundreds of years. Material in stable Kepler orbits was thus likely to hit the Earth–Moon system sometime later (because the Earth–Moon system's Kepler orbit around the Sun also remains stable). Estimates based on computer simulations of such an event suggest that some twenty percent of the original mass of Theia would have ended up as an orbiting ring of debris around Earth, and about half of this matter coalesced into the Moon. Earth would have gained significant amounts of angular momentum and mass from such a collision. Regardless of the speed and tilt of Earth's rotation before the impact, it would have experienced a day some five hours long after the impact, and Earth's equator and the Moon's orbit would have become coplanar.

Not all of the ring material need have been swept up right away: the thickened crust of the Moon's far side suggests the possibility that a second moon about 1,000 km (620 mi) in diameter formed in a Lagrange point of the Moon. The smaller moon may have remained in orbit for tens of millions of years.  As the two moons migrated outward from Earth, solar tidal effects would have made the Lagrange orbit unstable, resulting in a slow-velocity collision that "pancaked" the smaller moon onto what is now the far side of the Moon, adding material to its crust.

Lunar magma cannot pierce through the thick crust of the far side, causing fewer lunar maria, while the near side has a thin crust displaying the large maria visible from Earth.

Above a high resolution threshold for simulations, a study published in 2022 finds that giant impacts can immediately place a satellite with similar mass and iron content to the Moon into orbit far outside Earth's Roche limit. Even satellites that initially pass within the Roche limit can reliably and predictably survive, by being partially stripped and then torqued onto wider, stable orbits. Furthermore, the outer layers of these directly formed satellites are molten over cooler interiors and are composed of around 60% proto-Earth material. This could alleviate the tension between the Moon's Earth-like isotopic composition and the different signature expected for the impactor. Immediate formation opens up new options for the Moon's early orbit and evolution, including the possibility of a highly tilted orbit to explain the lunar inclination, and offers a simpler, single-stage scenario for the origin of the Moon.

## Composition

In 2001, a team at the Carnegie Institution of Washington reported that the rocks from the Apollo program carried an isotopic signature that was identical with rocks from Earth, and were different from almost all other bodies in the Solar System.

In 2014, a team in Germany reported that the Apollo samples had a slightly different isotopic signature from Earth rocks. The difference was slight, but statistically significant. One possible explanation is that Theia formed near Earth.

This empirical data showing close similarity of composition can be explained only by the standard giant-impact hypothesis, as it is extremely unlikely that two bodies prior to collision had such similar composition.

### Equilibration hypothesis

In 2007, researchers from the California Institute of Technology showed that the likelihood of Theia having an identical isotopic signature as Earth was very small (less than 1 percent). They proposed that in the aftermath of the giant impact, while Earth and the proto-lunar disc were molten and vaporised, the two reservoirs were connected by a common silicate vapor atmosphere and that the Earth–Moon system became homogenised by convective stirring while the system existed in the form of a continuous fluid. Such an "equilibration" between the post-impact Earth and the proto-lunar disc is the only proposed scenario that explains the isotopic similarities of the Apollo rocks with rocks from Earth's interior. For this scenario to be viable, however, the proto-lunar disc would have to endure for about 100 years. Work is ongoing to determine whether or not this is possible.

### Direct collision hypothesis

According to research (2012) to explain similar compositions of the Earth and the Moon based on simulations at the University of Bern by physicist Andreas Reufer and his colleagues, Theia collided directly with Earth instead of barely swiping it. The collision speed may have been higher than originally assumed, and this higher velocity may have totally destroyed Theia. According to this modification, the composition of Theia is not so restricted, making a composition of up to 50% water ice possible.

### Synestia hypothesis

One effort, in 2018, to homogenise the products of the collision was to energise the primary body by way of a greater pre-collision rotational speed.  This way, more material from the primary body would be spun off to form the Moon.  Further computer modelling determined that the observed result could be obtained by having the pre-Earth body spinning very rapidly, so much so that it formed a new celestial object which was given the name 'synestia'.  This is an unstable state that could have been generated by yet another collision to get the rotation spinning fast enough.  Further modelling of this transient structure has shown that the primary body spinning as a doughnut-shaped object (the synestia) existed for about a century (a very short time) before it cooled down and gave birth to Earth and the Moon.

### Terrestrial magma ocean hypothesis

Another model, in 2019, to explain the similarity of Earth and the Moon's compositions posits that shortly after Earth formed, it was covered by a sea of hot magma, while the impacting object was likely made of solid material. Modelling suggests that this would lead to the impact heating the magma much more than solids from the impacting object, leading to more material being ejected from the proto-Earth, so that about 80% of the Moon-forming debris originated from the proto-Earth. Many prior models had suggested 80% of the Moon coming from the impactor.

## Evidence

Indirect evidence for the giant impact scenario comes from rocks collected during the Apollo Moon landings, which show oxygen isotope ratios nearly identical to those of Earth. The highly anorthositic composition of the lunar crust, as well as the existence of KREEP-rich samples, suggest that a large portion of the Moon once was molten; and a giant impact scenario could easily have supplied the energy needed to form such a magma ocean. Several lines of evidence show that if the Moon has an iron-rich core, it must be a small one. In particular, the mean density, moment of inertia, rotational signature, and magnetic induction response of the Moon all suggest that the radius of its core is less than about 25% the radius of the Moon, in contrast to about 50% for most of the other terrestrial bodies. Appropriate impact conditions satisfying the angular momentum constraints of the Earth–Moon system yield a Moon formed mostly from the mantles of Earth and the impactor, while the core of the impactor accretes to Earth. Earth has the highest density of all the planets in the Solar System; the absorption of the core of the impactor body explains this observation, given the proposed properties of the early Earth and Theia.

Comparison of the zinc isotopic composition of lunar samples with that of Earth and Mars rocks provides further evidence for the impact hypothesis. Zinc is strongly fractionated when volatilised in planetary rocks, but not during normal igneous processes, so zinc abundance and isotopic composition can distinguish the two geological processes. Moon rocks contain more heavy isotopes of zinc, and overall less zinc, than corresponding igneous Earth or Mars rocks, which is consistent with zinc being depleted from the Moon through evaporation, as expected for the giant impact origin.

Collisions between ejecta escaping Earth's gravity and asteroids would have left impact heating signatures in stony meteorites; analysis based on assuming the existence of this effect has been used to date the impact event to 4.47 billion years ago, in agreement with the date obtained by other means.

Warm silica-rich dust and abundant SiO gas, products of high velocity impacts – over 10 km/s (6.2 mi/s) – between rocky bodies, have been detected by the Spitzer Space Telescope around the nearby (29 pc distant) young (~12 My old) star HD 172555 in the Beta Pictoris moving group. A belt of warm dust in a zone between 0.25AU and 2AU from the young star HD 23514 in the Pleiades cluster appears similar to the predicted results of Theia's collision with the embryonic Earth, and has been interpreted as the result of planet-sized objects colliding with each other. A similar belt of warm dust was detected around the star BD+20°307 (HIP 8920, SAO 75016).

On 1 November 2023, scientists reported that, according to computer simulations, remnants of Theia could be still visible inside the Earth as two giant anomalies of the Earth's mantle.

## Difficulties

This lunar origin hypothesis has some difficulties that have yet to be resolved. For example, the giant-impact hypothesis implies that a surface magma ocean would have formed following the impact. Yet there is no evidence that Earth ever had such a magma ocean and it is likely there exists material that has never been processed in a magma ocean.

### Composition

A number of compositional inconsistencies need to be addressed.

The ratios of the Moon's volatile elements are not explained by the giant-impact hypothesis. If the giant-impact hypothesis is correct, these ratios must be due to some other cause.

The presence of volatiles such as water trapped in lunar basalts and carbon emissions from the lunar surface is more difficult to explain if the Moon was caused by a high-temperature impact.

The iron oxide (FeO) content (13%) of the Moon, intermediate between that of Mars (18%) and the terrestrial mantle (8%), rules out most of the source of the proto-lunar material from Earth's mantle.

If the bulk of the proto-lunar material had come from an impactor, the Moon should be enriched in siderophilic elements, when, in fact, it is deficient in them.

The Moon's oxygen isotopic ratios are essentially identical to those of Earth. Oxygen isotopic ratios, which may be measured very precisely, yield a unique and distinct signature for each Solar System body. If a separate proto-planet Theia had existed, it probably would have had a different oxygen isotopic signature than Earth, as would the ejected mixed material.

The Moon's titanium isotope ratio (50Ti/47Ti) appears so close to Earth's (within 4 ppm), that little if any of the colliding body's mass could likely have been part of the Moon.

### Lack of a Venusian moon

If the Moon was formed by such an impact, it is possible that other inner planets also may have been subjected to comparable impacts. A moon that formed around Venus by this process would have been unlikely to escape. If such a moon-forming event had occurred there, a possible explanation of why the planet does not have such a moon might be that a second collision occurred that countered the angular momentum from the first impact. Another possibility is that the strong tidal forces from the Sun would tend to destabilise the orbits of moons around close-in planets. For this reason, if Venus's slow rotation rate began early in its history, any satellites larger than a few kilometers in diameter would likely have spiraled inwards and collided with Venus.

Simulations of the chaotic period of terrestrial planet formation suggest that impacts like those hypothesised to have formed the Moon were common. For typical terrestrial planets with a mass of 0.5 to 1 Earth masses, such an impact typically results in a single moon containing 4% of the host planet's mass. The inclination of the resulting moon's orbit is random, but this tilt affects the subsequent dynamic evolution of the system. For example, some orbits may cause the moon to spiral back into the planet. Likewise, the proximity of the planet to the star will also affect the orbital evolution. The net effect is that it is more likely for impact-generated moons to survive when they orbit more distant terrestrial planets and are aligned with the planetary orbit.

## Possible origin of Theia

In 2004, Princeton University mathematician Edward Belbruno and astrophysicist J. Richard Gott III proposed that Theia coalesced at the L4 or L5 Lagrangian point relative to Earth (in about the same orbit and about 60° ahead or behind), similar to a trojan asteroid. Two-dimensional computer models suggest that the stability of Theia's proposed trojan orbit would have been affected when its growing mass exceeded a threshold of approximately 10% of Earth's mass (the mass of Mars). In this scenario, gravitational perturbations by planetesimals ca

## Poin-Poin Kunci

- In 1898, George Darwin made the suggestion that Earth and the Moon were once a single body.
- The name of the hypothesised protoplanet is derived from the mythical Greek titan Theia , who gave birth to the Moon goddess Selene.
- Astronomers think the collision between Earth and Theia happened at about 4.4 to 4.45 billion years ago (bya); about 0.1 billion years after the Solar System began to form.
- In 2001, a team at the Carnegie Institution of Washington reported that the rocks from the Apollo program carried an isotopic signature that was identical with rocks from Earth, and were different from almost all other bodies in the Solar System.
- In 2007, researchers from the California Institute of Technology showed that the likelihood of Theia having an identical isotopic signature as Earth was very small (less than 1 percent).
- According to research (2012) to explain similar compositions of the Earth and the Moon based on simulations at the University of Bern by physicist Andreas Reufer and his colleagues, Theia collided directly with Earth instead of barely swiping it.

## Kesimpulan

Understanding Earth's past is not nostalgia; it is the key to understanding why our planet became a home for life. Every rock layer, mineral trace, and fossil is a page in the greatest history book ever written, and we have only read the first few chapters.

# Pricing Model SaaS: Flat, Tiered, atau Usage?


![Pricing Model SaaS — ilustrasi topik](/images/topics/saas.svg)
*Gambar: Pricing Model SaaS*

## Pendahuluan

Jika Anda diminta menyebut satu keputusan yang paling cepat mengubah pendapatan sebuah produk, jawabannya bukan fitur baru, bukan juga kampanye marketing—melainkan **harga**. Mengubah harga dari $19 menjadi $29 bisa menggandakan margin tanpa menambah satu baris kode. Sebaliknya, struktur harga yang salah bisa membuat pertumbuhan pengguna justru memperbesar kerugian.

Ironisnya, pricing adalah keputusan yang paling sering diambil secara asal: meniru kompetitor, menebak-nebak, atau memilih angka yang "terasa aman". Artikel ini membedah model-model pricing SaaS utama—flat-rate, tiered, per-seat, usage-based, dan hybrid—lengkap dengan kelebihan, kekurangan, serta prinsip memilih yang tepat untuk tahap bisnis Anda.

## Flat-Rate: Sederhana dan Jujur

Dalam model flat-rate, semua pelanggan membayar harga sama untuk seluruh fitur—misalnya $49/bulan, tanpa paket berbeda.

**Kelebihannya:** kesederhanaan absolut. Tidak ada kebingungan memilih paket, tidak ada friction keputusan, dan perhitungan pendapatan sangat mudah diprediksi. Untuk produk dengan nilai yang sama rata bagi semua pengguna, flat-rate jujur dan efisien.

**Kekurangannya:** ia meninggalkan uang di meja. Pelanggan besar yang bersedia membayar $200 hanya membayar $49, sementara pelanggan kecil yang hanya sanggup $10 terhalang masuk. Flat-rate cocok untuk tools dengan segmen pengguna homogen—misalnya alat khusus freelancer—tetapi sulit menskalakan untuk basis pelanggan yang beragam.

## Tiered: Standar Industri

Model bertingkat menawarkan beberapa paket (misalnya Starter, Pro, Business) dengan batasan fitur, kuota, atau level support yang meningkat. Inilah struktur yang paling umum dijumpai pada produk SaaS modern.

**Kelebihannya:** segmentasi alami. Paket murah menurunkan hambatan masuk; paket mahal menangkap surplus dari pelanggan bernilai tinggi. Struktur ini juga menciptakan jalur upgrade yang jelas seiring tumbuhnya pelanggan.

**Kekurangannya:** kompleksitas tersembunyi. Terlalu banyak paket membuat calon pembeli mengalami paralysis by analysis; terlalu banyak batasan artifisial (fitur dikunci seenaknya) memancing frustrasi. Praktik yang baik: maksimal 3–4 paket, dengan pemisah berbasis **nilai yang diterima**—bukan sekadar fitur yang disandera. Pertanyaan panduannya: "apa metrik yang tumbuh seiring pelanggan mendapat lebih banyak manfaat?" Bisa jumlah proyek, volume kontak, atau jumlah anggota tim.

## Per-Seat: Selaras dengan Ukuran Tim

Model per-seat mengenakan biaya per pengguna aktif—$15/pengguna/bulan, misalnya. Ia populer pada software kolaborasi karena biaya tumbuh otomatis saat tim pelanggan bertambah.

Keunggulannya adalah skalabilitas pendapatan yang elegan: pelanggan yang sukses akan memperbanyak kursus tanpa perlu negosiasi ulang. Kekurangannya, per-seat menciptakan hambatan adopsi internal—setiap tambahan kursus harus meyakinkan pengelola anggaran—dan sering memicu praktik sharing akun yang menggerogoti pendapatan. Banyak vendor kini beralih ke model berbasis *active user* atau *usage* untuk mengatasi kelemahan ini.


![Pricing Model SaaS — teknologi & produktivitas](/images/topics/teknologi-alt.svg)
*Gambar: Pricing Model SaaS*

## Usage-Based: Bayar Sebanding Pemakaian

Usage-based pricing (pay-as-you-go) menagih sesuai konsumsi nyata: per panggilan API, per gigabyte, per menit komputasi, atau per token AI. AWS, Twilio, dan penyedia API AI adalah contoh klasiknya.

**Kelebihannya:** keselarasan sempurna antara biaya dan nilai. Pelanggan baru tak perlu komitmen besar—mulai dari nol dan tumbuh seiring kebutuhan. Bagi vendor, pendapatan naik otomatis ketika pelanggan sukses. Model ini juga menurunkan hambatan percobaan secara dramatis.

**Kekurangannya:** ketidakpastian. Tagihan yang sulit diprediksi membuat pelanggan enterprise gelisah—tak ada CFO yang senang tagihan membengkak tanpa peringatan. Di sisi vendor, pendapatan fluktuatif menyulitkan perencanaan, dan perilaku optimasi pemakaian pelanggan dapat menekan pendapatan tanpa Anda sadari. Mitigasinya umum: sediakan simulasi biaya, alert kuota, dan opsi komitmen bulanan dengan diskon.

## Hybrid: Realita Praktik Terbaik

Perhatikan tren industri belakangan: mayoritas SaaS sukses memadukan beberapa model sekaligus. Pola yang lazim:

- **Basis langganan bertingkat** untuk prediktabilitas + **komponen usage** untuk skala (misalnya paket dasar sudah termasuk 1.000 kredit, sisanya dibayar sesuai pakai).
- **Platform fee + seat**, seperti banyak tools sales yang menagih akses platform per perusahaan plus kursus per pengguna.
- **Freemium atau trial + self-serve tiers untuk SMB, dan kontrak custom untuk enterprise.**

Hybrid memberi fleksibilitas menangkap beragam tipe pelanggan, tetapi tetap butuh disiplin agar struktur tak berubah menjadi labirin yang membingungkan.

## Prinsip Menentukan Harga yang Benar

Apa pun modelnya, prinsip-prinsip berikut berlaku universal:

1. **Berangkat dari nilai, bukan biaya.** Jika tool Anda menghemat pelanggan $500/bulan, harga $50 terasa murah; harga $150 masih masuk akal. Harga yang berbasis biaya server hampir selalu terlalu rendah.
2. **Pilih value metric yang tepat.** Satu-satunya variabel penentu harga haruslah hal yang tumbuh seiring nilai yang diterima pelanggan. Salah metric = pertumbuhan pelanggan tidak diikuti pertumbuhan pendapatan.
3. **Gunakan psikologi harga secukupnya.** Angka berakhiran 9 bekerja di B2C; di B2B profesional, angka bulat ($99 vs $100) sering lebih dipercaya.
4. **Selalu sediakan opsi premium.** Segmen kecil pelanggan bernilai tinggi biasanya menyumbang porsi pendapatan yang tidak proporsional.
5. **Naikkan harga dengan disiplin.** Uji kenaikan pada pelanggan baru dahulu, komunikasikan kepada pelanggan lama dengan transisi yang adil, dan pantau churn pasca-kenaikan.
6. **Perlakukan pricing sebagai eksperimen berkelanjutan.** Pasar berubah; struktur harga dua tahun lalu hampir pasti bukan yang optimal hari ini.

## Kesimpulan

Tidak ada model pricing yang objektif terbaik—yang ada hanya yang paling selaras dengan cara pelanggan Anda memperoleh nilai. Flat-rate unggul dalam kesederhanaan, tiered unggul dalam segmentasi, per-seat tumbuh bersama tim pelanggan, dan usage-based tumbuh bersama konsumsi nyata. Praktik terbaik masa kini kerap meramu semuanya dalam struktur hybrid yang tertata.

Yang tidak boleh dinegosiasikan adalah prinsipnya: harga berbasis nilai yang diterima, value metric yang tepat, struktur sesederhana mungkin, serta kesediaan bereksperimen dan merevisi. Pricing bukan keputusan sekali jadi melainkan sistem hidup—dan founder yang memperlakukannya demikian akan menemukan bahwa lever pendapatan terbesarnya ternyata tidak ada di dalam kode.

# SaaS Pricing Models: Flat, Tiered, or Usage-Based?


![SaaS Pricing Models — ilustrasi topik](/images/topics/saas.svg)
*Image: SaaS Pricing Models*

## Introduction

If you had to name the single decision that most rapidly changes a product's revenue, it wouldn't be a new feature or a marketing campaign—it would be **price**. Moving from $19 to $29 can double margins without adding a line of code. Conversely, the wrong pricing structure can turn user growth into accelerating losses.

Ironically, pricing is also the decision most often made carelessly: copying competitors, guessing, or picking numbers that "feel safe." This article breaks down the major SaaS pricing models—flat-rate, tiered, per-seat, usage-based, and hybrid—with their strengths, weaknesses, and principles for choosing what fits your stage of business.

## Flat-Rate: Simple and Honest

In flat-rate pricing, every customer pays the same price for full access—say $49/month with no plan variations.

**Strengths:** absolute simplicity. No package confusion, no decision friction, and highly predictable revenue math. For products delivering roughly equal value to every user, flat-rate is honest and efficient.

**Weaknesses:** it leaves money on the table. A large customer willing to pay $200 pays only $49, while a small customer who can afford just $10 is blocked out. Flat-rate suits tools serving homogeneous segments—for instance, freelancer-only software—but struggles to scale across diverse customer bases.

## Tiered: The Industry Standard

Tiered pricing offers several packages (say Starter, Pro, Business) with escalating feature limits, quotas, or support levels. It's the structure you'll encounter on most modern SaaS products.

**Strengths:** natural segmentation. Cheap packages lower the entry barrier; expensive packages capture surplus from high-value customers. Tiers also create an obvious upgrade path as customers grow.

**Weaknesses:** hidden complexity. Too many packages trigger choice paralysis; too many artificial restrictions (arbitrarily locked features) breed frustration. Good practice: three to four packages maximum, separated by **delivered value** rather than held-hostage features. The guiding question: "what metric grows as the customer gets more benefit?" It might be project count, contact volume, or team size.

## Per-Seat: Aligned with Team Size

Per-seat pricing charges per active user—$15/user/month, for example. Collaboration software favors it because revenue grows automatically as customer teams expand.

Its elegant strength is revenue scaling: successful customers buy more seats without renegotiation. The drawbacks: per-seat creates internal adoption friction—every added seat needs budget approval—and often triggers account-sharing that quietly erodes revenue. Many vendors are shifting toward active-user or usage models to counter these weaknesses.


![SaaS Pricing Models — teknologi & produktivitas](/images/topics/teknologi-alt.svg)
*Image: SaaS Pricing Models*

## Usage-Based: Pay for What You Use

Usage-based pricing (pay-as-you-go) bills by actual consumption: per API call, gigabyte stored, compute minute, or AI token. AWS, Twilio, and AI API providers are classic examples.

**Strengths:** perfect alignment between cost and value. New customers need no big commitment—they start at zero and grow with their needs. For vendors, revenue rises automatically when customers succeed. This model also dramatically lowers trial friction.

**Weaknesses:** unpredictability. Hard-to-forecast bills make enterprise buyers nervous—no CFO enjoys invoices ballooning without warning. On the vendor side, fluctuating revenue complicates planning, and customers optimizing their usage can quietly shrink your income. Common mitigations include cost simulators, quota alerts, and committed monthly plans with discounts.

## Hybrid: How Practice Actually Works

Notice the recent industry trend: most successful SaaS companies blend multiple models. Common patterns:

- **Tiered subscription base + usage component** for predictability plus scale (a base plan including 1,000 credits, with overage billed per use).
- **Platform fee + seats**, like many sales tools charging company-level platform access plus per-user seats.
- **Freemium or trials + self-serve tiers for SMBs, custom contracts for enterprise.**

Hybrid structures capture diverse customer types—but still demand discipline so the result doesn't become a confusing maze.

## Principles for Getting Pricing Right

Whatever model you choose, these principles apply universally:

1. **Start from value, not cost.** If your tool saves customers $500/month, $50 feels cheap and $150 remains reasonable. Pricing based on server costs is almost always too low.
2. **Pick the right value metric.** The single variable determining price should be something that grows alongside the customer's received benefit. Wrong metric = customer growth without revenue growth.
3. **Use price psychology sparingly.** Charm prices ending in 9 work in B2C; in professional B2B, round numbers ($100 vs $99) often inspire more trust.
4. **Always offer a premium option.** A small segment of high-value customers typically contributes a disproportionate share of revenue.
5. **Raise prices with discipline.** Test increases on new customers first, transition existing ones fairly, and monitor post-increase churn.
6. **Treat pricing as ongoing experimentation.** Markets change; a two-year-old pricing structure is almost certainly not today's optimum.

## Conclusion

There is no objectively best pricing model—only the one most aligned with how your customers receive value. Flat-rate wins on simplicity, tiered on segmentation, per-seat grows with customer teams, and usage-based grows with real consumption. Today's best practice often blends them into well-designed hybrids.

What's non-negotiable are the principles: price against delivered value, choose the right value metric, keep structure as simple as possible, and stay willing to experiment and revise. Pricing isn't a one-time decision—it's a living system—and founders who treat it that way discover their biggest revenue lever was never inside the code.

# Prompt Engineering: Seni Bertanya ke AI


![Prompt Engineering — ilustrasi topik](/images/topics/ai.svg)
*Gambar: Prompt Engineering*

Ada satu keterampilan baru yang diam-diam menjadi sangat berharga di era AI: **prompt engineering**, yaitu seni merumuskan instruksi agar model bahasa menghasilkan keluaran terbaik. Kabar baiknya, ini bukan ilmu roket. Tidak perlu bisa coding — cukup ubah cara Anda bertanya. Artikel ini membahas prinsip-prinsip inti beserta contoh nyata yang bisa langsung Anda coba.

## Mengapa Cara Bertanya Begitu Menentukan

Model bahasa seperti ChatGPT bekerja dengan menimbang kemungkinan jawaban berdasarkan semua informasi yang ia miliki: prompt Anda plus pengetahuannya dari pelatihan. Prompt yang kabur memaksa model menebak maksud Anda — dan tebakannya mungkin meleset.

Bandingkan dua prompt ini:

- **Vague**: *"Tulis tentang marketing."* → Hasilnya artikel generik yang mungkin tidak relevan sama sekali.
- **Spesifik**: *"Tulis draf email 150 kata untuk mengajak 500 pelanggan lama mencoba fitur baru kami, nada ramah profesional, sertakan tawaran diskon 20% dan batas waktu akhir bulan."* → Hasilnya langsung mendekati kebutuhan Anda.

Perbedaan hasilnya bisa drastis meski usaha mengetiknya hanya bertambah satu menit.

## Prinsip 1: Spesifik dan Beri Konteks

Jangan biarkan model menebak asumsi. Sertakan detail yang akan Anda berikan kepada asisten manusia baru: audiens siapa, tujuan apa, gaya seperti apa, dan kendala apa pun.

Contoh: alih-alih *"jelaskan fotosintesis"*, tulis *"jelaskan fotosintesis kepada anak SMP dalam 200 kata menggunakan analogi dapur"*. Model kini tahu tingkat bahasa, panjang, dan pendekatannya.

## Prinsip 2: Tetapkan Format Keluaran

Model sangat patuh soal struktur — selama Anda memintanya. Ingin jawaban berupa tabel? Daftar bernomor? Maksimal lima poin? JSON? Sebutkan langsung. Ini sangat berguna saat hasil AI akan dipakai lanjutan, misalnya dimasukkan ke spreadsheet atau sistem lain.

## Prinsip 3: Gunakan Role Prompting

Memberi peran membantu mengarahkan nada dan kedalaman jawaban:

- *"Anda adalah editor senior. Kritik draf artikel saya berikut dengan tegas namun membangun."*
- *"Sebagai guru matematika SMA, jelaskan konsep turunan tanpa notasi rumit."*

Peran yang jelas membuat model memilih kosakata dan kerangka berpikir yang sesuai.


![Prompt Engineering — teknologi & produktivitas](/images/topics/teknologi-alt.svg)
*Gambar: Prompt Engineering*

## Prinsip 4: Tunjukkan Contoh (Few-shot)

Salah satu trik paling ampuh: beri satu hingga tiga contoh input-output yang Anda inginkan sebelum memberi tugas sesungguhnya. Misalnya Anda ingin produk ditulis ulang dengan gaya tertentu — tunjukkan dua contoh sebelum-dan-sesudah, lalu minta model menerapkan pola yang sama pada data berikutnya. Model menangkap pola gaya jauh lebih andal lewat contoh daripada lewat deskripsi.

## Prinsip 5: Iterasi, Jangan Berharap Sempurna Sekali Jalan

Prompt hebat jarang lahir sekali ketik. Perlakui percakapan sebagai proses penyempurnaan:

1. Mulai dari prompt sederhana.
2. Periksa hasilnya, temukan apa yang kurang pas.
3. Perbaiki dengan instruksi tambahan: *"Lebih ringkas", "Ganti sudut pandang menjadi pembeli", "Tambahkan data pendukung"*.
4. Bila sudah bagus, simpan prompt tersebut sebagai template untuk digunakan ulang.

## Studi Mini: Memperbaiki Prompt Langkah demi Langkah

Mari lihat evolusi satu prompt nyata. Tugas: membuat deskripsi produk sepatu lari.

- **Versi 1**: *"Tulis deskripsi produk sepatu lari."* → Hasil generik, bisa untuk merek mana pun.
- **Versi 2**: *"Tulis deskripsi 80 kata untuk sepatu lari ringan berpelapis busa responsif, target pelari pemula, nada semangat."* → Sudah spesifik dan terasa hidup.
- **Versi 3**: menambahkan contoh gaya dari deskripsi produk lain yang disukai manajemen, plus permintaan format: kalimat pembuka menarik, tiga poin keunggulan, penutup ajakan. → Hasil siap pakai tanpa revisi besar.

Perhatikan polanya: setiap iterasi menambahkan satu jenis informasi — detail produk, audiens dan nada, lalu contoh dan struktur. Anda tidak perlu menulis prompt panjang sejak awal; bangun bertahap dan amati apa yang benar-benar mengubah kualitas keluaran.

## Kesalahan Umum yang Perlu Dihindari

- **Terlalu banyak tugas sekaligus.** "Ringkas artikel ini, terjemahkan, lalu buat 10 caption Instagram" — pecah menjadi langkah terpisah agar tiap hasil berkualitas.
- **Mengasumsikan model tahu konteks Anda.** Nama proyek internal atau singkatan kantor tak akan dimengerti tanpa penjelasan.
- **Menerima jawaban pertama mentah-mentah.** Selalu baca ulang; minta revisi bila perlu.
- **Prompt negatif berlebihan.** Daripada daftar panjang "jangan lakukan ini", lebih efektif menyatakan positif apa yang Anda inginkan.

Satu kebiasaan tambahan yang membedakan pengguna mahir: mereka menyimpan prompt yang berhasil. Buat dokumen pribadi berisi template untuk tugas rutin — merangkum rapat, menyusun caption, mengevaluasi ide. Setiap kali menemukan rumusan yang bekerja baik, salin ke sana beserta catatan konteksnya. Dalam beberapa bulan, Anda memiliki "perpustakaan prompt" yang membuat pekerjaan berulang selesai dalam hitungan detik.

## Kesimpulan

Prompt engineering adalah jembatan komunikasi antara niat Anda dan kemampuan mesin. Resep dasarnya: spesifik, beri konteks, tetapkan format, gunakan peran, tunjukkan contoh, dan iterasi sampai puas. Semakin baik Anda merumuskan permintaan, semakin besar nilai yang bisa Anda petik dari AI — sering kali bedanya hanya beberapa kalimat tambahan dalam prompt. Mulailah praktik hari ini dengan menyusun ulang satu prompt biasa Anda menjadi prompt yang lengkap, dan rasakan bedanya.

# Prompt Engineering: The Art of Asking AI


![Prompt Engineering — ilustrasi topik](/images/topics/ai.svg)
*Image: Prompt Engineering*

One quietly valuable skill has emerged in the AI era: **prompt engineering** — the craft of phrasing instructions so language models produce their best possible output. The good news: this isn't rocket science. You don't need to code; you just need to change how you ask. This article covers the core principles with real examples you can apply immediately.

## Why Wording Matters So Much

Language models like ChatGPT weigh what to answer based on everything available: your prompt plus their training knowledge. A vague prompt forces the model to guess your intent — and the guess may miss badly.

Compare these two prompts:

- **Vague**: *"Write about marketing."* → You get generic filler that may be entirely irrelevant.
- **Specific**: *"Write a 150-word draft email inviting 500 existing customers to try our new feature. Friendly-professional tone, include a 20% discount offer and an end-of-month deadline."* → The output lands close to what you actually need.

The results differ dramatically even though typing the better prompt took one extra minute.

## Principle 1: Be Specific and Add Context

Don't leave assumptions to chance. Include the details you'd give a new human assistant: who the audience is, what the goal is, what style you want, and any constraints.

Example: instead of *"explain photosynthesis"*, write *"explain photosynthesis to a middle-schooler in 200 words using a kitchen analogy."* Now the model knows the language level, length, and approach.

## Principle 2: Define the Output Format

Models are highly obedient about structure — if you ask. Want a table? Numbered list? Five bullet points maximum? JSON? Say so explicitly. This matters especially when AI output feeds into something else, like a spreadsheet or another system.

## Principle 3: Use Role Prompting

Assigning a persona steers tone and depth:

- *"You are a senior editor. Critique my article draft firmly but constructively."*
- *"As a high school math teacher, explain derivatives without heavy notation."*

A clear role makes the model choose vocabulary and thinking frameworks that fit.


![Prompt Engineering — teknologi & produktivitas](/images/topics/teknologi-alt.svg)
*Image: Prompt Engineering*

## Principle 4: Show Examples (Few-shot)

One of the most powerful tricks: provide one to three input-output examples before giving the real task. If you want product descriptions rewritten in a particular style, show two before-and-after samples, then ask the model to apply the same pattern to new data. Models pick up style far more reliably from examples than from descriptions.

## Principle 5: Iterate — Don't Expect Perfection First Try

Great prompts rarely appear in one keystroke. Treat each conversation as refinement:

1. Start with a simple prompt.
2. Inspect the result and spot what's off.
3. Correct with follow-ups: *"Make it shorter," "Switch perspective to the buyer," "Add supporting data."*
4. Once it's good, save that prompt as a reusable template.

## A Mini Case Study: Improving a Prompt Step by Step

Let's watch one real prompt evolve. Task: writing a product description for running shoes.

- **Version 1**: *"Write a product description for running shoes."* → Generic output that could fit any brand.
- **Version 2**: *"Write an 80-word description for lightweight running shoes with responsive foam cushioning, targeting beginner runners, energetic tone."* → Specific and alive.
- **Version 3**: add a style example from product copy management already likes, plus a format request: catchy opener, three bullet benefits, call-to-action close. → Output ready to ship without major revision.

Notice the pattern: each iteration adds one kind of information — product details, audience and tone, then examples and structure. You don't need to write long prompts from the start; build them incrementally and observe what actually changes output quality.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

- **Cramming multiple tasks together.** "Summarize this article, translate it, then write 10 Instagram captions" — split these into separate steps so each gets full quality.
- **Assuming shared context.** Internal project names or office abbreviations mean nothing without explanation.
- **Accepting the first draft blindly.** Always reread; request revisions when needed.
- **Overloading on negatives.** Rather than a long list of "don't do X", state positively what you do want.

## Conclusion

Prompt engineering is the communication bridge between your intent and a machine's capability. The basic recipe: be specific, give context, define format, assign roles, show examples, and iterate until satisfied. The better you phrase requests, the more value you extract from AI — often the difference is just a few extra sentences in the prompt. Start practicing today by rewriting one ordinary prompt into a complete one, and feel the difference.

# Kosakata Restoran: Pesan Makan Tanpa Gugup di Jepang


![Kosakata Restoran — ilustrasi topik](/images/topics/percakapan.svg)
*Gambar: Kosakata Restoran*

Pintu restoran terbuka, dan seluruh ruangan berseru serempak: "*Irasshaimase!*". Anda berdiri di ambang pintu, otak mendadak kosong, dan satu-satunya kata yang keluar adalah... "halo".

Adegan ini terjadi setiap hari pada jutaan wisatawan. Padahal makan di restoran Jepang adalah pengalaman salah satu yang paling ramah bagi pemula: stafnya terlatih sopan, menunya bergambar, dan prosesnya sangat terstruktur. Yang kurang cuma satu — **bekal kosakata** yang tepat supaya momen paling harapan liburan Anda tidak berubah jadi sesi panik.

Artikel ini merangkum kalimat-kalimat kunci dari masuk sampai bayar, plus penjelasan kenapa menu di Jepang terasa seperti teka-teki — dan cara memecahkannya.

## Kenapa Restoran Jepang Terasa Berbeda

Sedikit konteks dulu, karena ini menjelaskan banyak hal. Bahasa Jepang dituturkan sekitar **123 juta orang**, hampir semuanya di Jepang sendiri — artinya, kemampuan bahasa Inggris di luar kota besar bisa sangat bervariasi. Persiapan kosakata bukan opsi, melainkan kebutuhan.

Yang kedua lebih halus tapi penting: bahasa Jepang punya **sistem kehormatan (*keigo*) yang kompleks** — bentuk kata kerja dan kosakata khusus untuk menandai status pembicara dan pendengar. Staf restoran akan menyambut Anda dengan bahasa kehormatan tingkat tinggi, dan meski sebagai pelanggan Anda tak wajib membalas dengan keigo penuh, mengenali pola-polanya membuat telinga Anda tidak kaget. *Irasshaimase* itu sebenarnya bentuk hormat dari kata kerja *irassharu* — "datang/hadir". Anda sedang dihormati; tidak perlu panik.

Dan yang ketiga: bahasa Jepang adalah bahasa ***aglutinatif*** berpola **subjek-objek-predikat** dengan partikel penanda fungsi. Kabar baiknya, dalam situasi restoran Anda nyaris tidak butuh struktur kalimat rumit. Frasa pendek + kata bantu = cukup. Restoran adalah arena latihan bahasa paling ramah di Jepang.

## Saat Masuk: Merespons Irasshaimase

Begitu melangkah masuk, Anda akan disambut *Irasshaimase!* atau *Irasshai!* — artinya "selamat datang". Ini seruan staf, bukan pertanyaan, jadi Anda **tidak wajib menjawab**. Senyum, anggukan kecil, atau balas santai dengan *"Kon'nichiwa"* sudah lebih dari cukup.

Beberapa detik kemudian biasanya staf datang menunjukkan tempat duduk, atau bertanya berapa orang. Di sinilah angka menyelamatkan:

- **Hitori** (一人) — satu orang,
- **Futari** (二人) — dua orang,
- **San-nin** (三人) — tiga orang,
- **Yonin** (四人) — empat orang.

Atau cara paling ampuh: tunjukkan jari Anda sambil tersenyum. Serius — kombinasi jari + senyum bekerja di 99% restoran Jepang.

Kalau Anda ingin memilih meja atau bertanya soal reservasi: *Yoyaku shita ___ desu* ("Saya ada reservasi atas nama ___").

## Membaca Menu: Tiga Lapisan Aksara dan Satu Jebakan

Menu Jepang bisa tampak menyeramkan karena campuran tiga sistem tulisan: **kanji** untuk nama hidangan utama, **hiragana** untuk potongan-potongan gramatikal, dan **katakana** untuk kata serapan asing. Kabar baik: katakana adalah teman terbaik Anda di restoran, karena semua makanan asing ditulis dengannya — ハンバーガー (*hanbāgā*, hamburger), ピザ (*piza*, pizza), サラダ (*sarada*, salad).

Tapi waspadai jebakan bernama ***wasei-eigo*** — "bahasa Inggris buatan Jepang": kata berakar Inggris yang maknanya dimodifikasi. *Manshon* (mansion) bukan mansion mewah tapi apartemen; dan di dunia kuliner, beberapa istilah berjalan sendiri jalannya. Jangan asumsikan bunyi Inggris = makna Inggris.

Beberapa kata menu yang layak dihafal:

- **Osusume** (おすすめ) — rekomendasi/special of the day,
- **Niku** (肉) — daging; **sakana** (魚) — ikan; **yasai** (野菜) — sayur,
- **Butaniku** — daging babi; **gyūniku** — daging sapi; **toriniku** — ayam,
- **Mizu** (水) — air; **o-cha** (お茶) — teh; **bīru** (ビール) — bir,
- **Ōmori** (大盛り) — porsi besar; **shōmori** (小盛り) — porsi kecil,
- **Dezāto** (デザート) — pencuci mulut.

Perhatikan juga prefiks **o-** atau **go-** di depan banyak kata — itu tanda kehormatan. *O-mizu* dan *mizu* sama-sama air; versi dengan *o-* lebih lembut dan lazim diucapkan staf.

## Kalimat Kunci untuk Memesan

Inilah inti senjatanya. Empat kalimat ini menutupi 90% situasi pemesanan:

**"Menyū o onegaishimasu."** (メニューをお願いします) — "Menu-nya, tolong." Frasa sakti ***onegaishimasu*** ("tolong/mohon") akan Anda pakai berkali-kali sepanjang malam. Ini formula ajaib: **[barang yang diinginkan] + o + onegaishimasu**.

**"Kore o kudasai."** (これをください) — "Ini, tolong." Sambil menunjuk gambar atau tulisan di menu. ***Kudasai*** adalah versi santai dari *onegaishimasu* — dua-duanya benar, keduanya disukai staf.

**"Osusume wa nan desu ka."** (おすすめは何ですか) — "Apa rekomendasinya?" Pertanyaan pembuka pintu: staf biasanya antusias menjawab dan kadang langsung menunjukkan hidangan favoritnya.

**"Eigo no menyū wa arimasu ka."** (英語のメニューはありますか) — "Apakah ada menu bahasa Inggris?" Tidak ada rasa malu dalam pertanyaan ini — banyak restoran wisata menyediakannya.

Untuk jumlah porsi, gunakan penghitung ***ninmae*** (人前, "porsi untuk ... orang"): *"Ramen futari-mae o onegaishimasu"* — "dua porsi ramen, tolong."

### Pertanyaan Penyelamat

Beberapa kalimat tambahan yang sering menyelamatkan malam:

- **"Kore wa nan desu ka."** (これは何ですか) — "Ini apa?" — sambil menunjuk menu.
- **"___ ga arimasen."** — "___ habis/tidak ada" — kalimat staf; dengarkan kata *arimasen* sebagai alarm untuk memilih menu lain.
- **"Sumimasen!"** (すみません) — kata serbaguna nomor satu Jepang: "permisi". Panggil staf, minta bantuan, minta maaf — satu kata untuk segalanya.
- **"O-kaikei onegaishimasu."** — simpan ini untuk nanti; kita bahas sebentar lagi.

## Jenis Restoran, Jenis Kosakata

Kosakata restoran Jepang bukan satu paket seragam — tiap jenis tempat makan punya ritual dan perbendaharaannya sendiri. Mengenalnya membuat Anda siap di mana saja:

**Izakaya** — pub makan ala Jepang, surganya menu kecil-kecil (*otsumami*) dan minuman. Kata kuncinya *kanpai!* (sikat gelas, "bersulang!") dan... waspadai ***otoshi***: hidangan kecil kejutan yang otomatis datang sebagai "biaya tempat duduk" dan masuk tagihan. Itu normal, bukan penipuan. Pesan minuman pertama dengan *"Toriaezu bīru!"* ("dulu bir aja") dan Anda langsung terdengar seperti orang lokal.

**Kaiten-zushi** (sushi berpiring berjalan) — piring sushi lewat di konveyor; Anda ambil sesuka hati dan kasir menghitung **piring-piringnya**. Kosakata penting: *aburi* (dibakar-sebagian), *agari* (istilah dalam untuk teh hijau), dan *gari* (acar jahe pembersih lidah). Bayar dengan menyebut jumlah warna piring.

**Family restaurant** (famiresu) — restoran keluarga 24 jam bergaya barat-jepang. Ada *drink bar* (refill), menu anak, dan pelayanan tanpa tekanan. Tempat paling aman bagi pemula total.

**Ramen shop** — sering memakai mesin tiket di pintu (bahas sebentar lagi), kursi meja panjang, dan etika cepat: makan saat masih panas, slurping justru diperbolehkan.

**Depachika dan food court** — basement department store yang menjual lauk premium; kata kunci *omochikaeri* (bungkus pulang) dan *shōhinkibi* (tanggal kedaluwarsa hari ini — diskon sore hari!).


![Kosakata Restoran](/images/topics/bahasa-jepang-alt.svg)
*Gambar: Kosakata Restoran*

## Skenario Nyata: Satu Malam di Ramen Shop

Mari gabungkan semuanya dalam skenario nyata. Anda masuk ke ramen shop kecil di Tokyo:

Di pintu ada mesin tiket. Layarnya bergambar: *Shōyu ramen* (880 yen), *Miso ramen* (920), *Tonkotsu* (900). Masukkan uang kertas, tekan tombol miso, plus tombol *chāshū aji-tamago* (tambahan daging + telur). Mesin mengeluarkan dua kupon. Anda duduk di meja panjang dan menyerahkan kupon kepada staf sambil berkata: *"Onegaishimasu."*

Beberapa menit kemudian staf bertanya singkat: *"Katame de daijōbu desu ka?"* — "kekataman (mi agak keras) boleh?" Anda ingat kosakata tingkat kematangan mi: *yawarakame* (lembut), *futsū* (normal), *katame* (keras). Jawab: *"Hai, katame de!"*

Ramen datang bersup panas. Ucapkan pelan *"Itadakimasu"*, lalu kerjakan: aduk sedikit, cicip kuah dulu, baru habiskan. Di tengah suapan Anda ingin tambahan bawang putih — cukup angkat tangan dan panggil *"Sumimasen!"* lalu tunjuk wadah bumbu di meja: *"Kore o onegaishimasu."*

Selesai. Angkat kepala dari mangkuk, ucapkan *"Gochisōsama deshita"* pada staf, taruh mangkuk di rak pencuci, dan pergi tanpa perlu membayar lagi — semua sudah lunas lewat kupon tadi. Seluruh interaksi hanya butuh lima frasa. Inilah kenapa restoran adalah titik awal terbaik melatih bahasa: strukturnya terbatas, responsnya bisa diprediksi, dan kesalahan tetap tersenyum.



## Selama Makan: Kata-Kata yang Menghangatkan

Sebelum suapan pertama, orang Jepang mengucapkan ***Itadakimasu*** — secara harfiah "saya menerima (hidup ini)". Bukan sekadar "selamat makan", melainkan ungkapan syukur pada makanan dan siapa yang menyiapkannya. Ucapkan pelan, tak perlu dramatis — tapi ucapkan.

Saat mencicipi, **"Oishii!"** (美味しい) — "lezat!" — adalah komplimen paling universal dan paling disukai koki. Versi lebih formalnya *oishikatta desu* untuk akhir makan. Staf yang mendengar *oishii* sambil tersenyum tahu pekerjaannya berhasil.

Di tengah makan, kalau butuh sesuatu: *Mizu o onegaishimasu* (airnya tolong) atau *O-hashi o onegaishimasu* (sumpitnya tolong). Dan ketika selesai, tutup dengan ***Gochisōsama deshita*** — "terima kasih atas jamuan". Ini pasangan resmi dari *itadakimasu*, dan mengucapkannya sambil bangkit dari kursi adalah sentuhan budaya yang tak pernah gagal menghangatkan suasana.

### Etika Kecil yang Bernilai Besar

Beberapa hal non-verbal yang membuat staf jatuh cinta padamu: jangan menempelkan sumpit vertikal ke dalam nasi (itu ritual pemakaman); jangan berpindah-pindah piring dari posisi awalnya; dan di banyak restoran ramen, pesan lewat mesin tiket otomatis di pintu masuk — tunjukkan kuponnya kepada staf, tanpa perlu bicara sama sekali.

Soal tip: di Jepang **tidak ada budaya tip**. Biaya servis sudah termasuk, dan meninggalkan uang receh di meja justru bisa membingungkan staf yang mengejar Anda untuk mengembalikannya. Ucapan *gochisōsama* adalah tip tertinggi mereka.

## Membayar: Momen Paling Sederhana

Kabar baik terakhir: proses bayar di Jepang luar biasa sederhana. Di banyak restoran kasual, Anda bayar **di kasir dekat pintu** — bukan di meja. Cukup berdiri di kasir dan ucapkan:

**"O-kaikei onegaishimasu."** (お会計お願いします) — "Pembayarannya, tolong."

Alternatif yang setara: *O-kanjō onegaishimasu*. Staf akan menampilkan struk atau menghitung total, Anda bayar — tunai masih rajaa di restoran kecil, jadi siapkan uang kertas dan koin.

Satu frasa penyelamat terakhir: **"Bunkatsu dekimasu ka?"** — "Bisa dibagi (tagihannya)?" — berguna saat makan rombongan. Dan setelah transaksi selesai, *Arigatō gozaimasu* menutup malam dengan sempurna.

Perhatikan bahwa *o-kaikei* dan *o-kanjō* kembali memakai prefiks kehormatan *o-* — konsistensi bahasa hormat dari pintu masuk sampai pintu keluar adalah identitas layanan Jepang.

## Kosakata untuk Situasi Sulit

Sekarang lapisan lanjutan: kalimat untuk momen tak ideal — karena justru di situ bahasa paling dibutuhkan.

**Alergi dan batasan makanan.** Kalimat penyelamat: *"___ arerugī ga arimasu"* ("saya alergi ___") — isi dengan *ebi* (udang), *kani* (kepiting), *tamago* (telur), *gyūniku* (daging sapi). Untuk kebutuhan halal atau vegetarian, frasa yang lebih panjang diperlukan: *"Niku wa tabemasen"* ("saya tidak makan daging"). Di Jepang, kaldu ikan (*dashi*) sering menyamar di hidangan yang tampak sayuran — jangan ragu bertanya *"Dashi wa irimasu ka?"*.

**Pesanan salah datang.** Tunjuk dengan tenang dan katakan *"Chigaimasu"* ("ini berbeda") sambil menunjukkan menu. Staf Jepang terlatih meminta maaf dan mengganti cepat — tidak perlu nada tinggi; ketenangan adalah bahasa keluhan paling efektif di sana.

**Meminta sesuatu diganti.** *"Mizu o kudasai"* versi sopannya adalah *"O-mizu o itadakemasu ka."* Terlalu panjang? *Sumimasen* + gestur tetap bekerja. Prinsip umumnya: makin formal kalimat, makin hormat — tapi frasa pendek pun hampir selalu diterima dengan senyum.

**Hilang kupon mesin tiket.** Di ramen shop, tunjukkan tangan kosong dan ucapkan *"Kippu o nakushimashita"* ("kupon saya hilang"). Biasanya staf membantu dengan sabar — dan ini pelajaran penting: mengaku kesalahan secara jujur dalam bahasa sederhana selalu diterima lebih baik daripada pura-pura tidak terjadi apa-apa.

**Butuh waktu lebih lama memesan.** Tekan tombol kejujuran universal: *"Chotto matte kudasai"* ("mohon tunggu sebentar") sambil tersenyum. Tidak ada staf Jepang yang menekan pelanggan buru-buru.

Perhatikan benang merahnya: dalam situasi sulit, **kesederhanaan + kesopanan + gestur** menyelesaikan 95% masalah. Anda tidak perlu pidato — cukup satu frasa yang tepat, disampaikan dengan sikap yang benar.

Sebagai penutup bagian ini, satu saran latihan yang terbukti efektif: **role-play mandiri**. Sebelum berangkat, jalankan simulasi lengkap di kepala atau bersama teman — dari masuk pintu sampai membayar — menggunakan semua frasa di artikel ini. Ucapkan nyaring. Otomatisasi mulut sama pentingnya dengan hafalan telinga: frasa yang pernah Anda ucapkan tiga kali akan jauh lebih mudah keluar dalam situasi asli daripada frasa yang baru dibaca sepuluh kali.

Terakhir, manfaatkan teknologi sebagai jaring pengaman tanpa menjadikannya tongkat crutch. Simpan gambar menu favorit, aktifkan aplikasi kamus luring, dan pelajari fitur terjemahan kamera ponsel — berguna untuk label harga atau catatan kecil di restoran. Tapi gunakan hanya saat macet: setiap kali Anda berhasil menyelesaikan satu transaksi dengan bahasa sendiri, ketergantungan pada layar berkurang sedikit — dan itulah kemajuan yang sesungguhnya.

Belajar satu skenario dengan sungguh-sungguh ternyata membuka banyak pintu sekaligus — itulah kenapa memulai dari restoran adalah keputusan belajar yang cerdas.

## Kesimpulan

Makan di restoran Jepang ternyata bukan ujian bahasa, melainkan rutinitas yang bisa dipelajari dalam satu sore: sambut *irasshaimase* dengan senyum, tunjukkan angka dengan jari, pesan dengan *kore o kudasai* dan *onegaishimasu*, puji dengan *oishii*, tutup dengan *gochisōsama deshita*, dan bayar dengan *o-kaikei onegaishimasu*. Sepuluh frasa itu sudah membuat Anda pelanggan yang jauh lebih percaya diri daripada 90% turis.

Lebih dari itu, restoran adalah laboratorium bahasa terbaik di Jepang: situasinya terstruktur, responsnya terprediksi, dan kesalahannya selalu diampuni dengan senyum. Setiap kali Anda berhasil memesan tanpa bantuan Google Translate, keberanian bahasa Anda naik satu level — dan level itu akan terbawa ke konbini, stasiun kereta, dan percakapan berikutnya.

Jadi latihlah sepuluh frasa itu sebelum penerbangan. Nanti di Tokyo, ketika seluruh ruangan berseru *irasshaimase*, Anda tidak akan membeku — Anda akan tersenyum, duduk, dan mulai memesan seperti orang yang memang tinggal di sana.

en.contentMarkdown:
---
title: "Restaurant Vocabulary: Ordering Food Without Panic"
excerpt: "From 'irasshaimase' to 'o-kaikei onegaishimasu' — key phrases, menu-reading tricks, and small etiquette so dining in Japan feels confident."
meta_title: "Japanese Restaurant Vocabulary: Order Food Confidently"
meta_description: "A complete guide to Japanese restaurant vocabulary: ordering phrases, reading menus, paying the bill, and dining etiquette for stress-free travel."
category: "japanese-language"
tags: ["japanese vocabulary","japanese restaurants","japanese conversation","japan travel","learn japanese"]

# Restaurant Vocabulary: Ordering Food Without Panic


![Restaurant Vocabulary — ilustrasi topik](/images/topics/percakapan.svg)
*Image: Restaurant Vocabulary*

The door opens and the entire room shouts in unison: "*Irasshaimase!*". You stand at the threshold, your brain goes blank, and the only word that escapes is... "hello."

This scene plays out daily for millions of travelers. Yet eating at a Japanese restaurant is actually one of the friendliest experiences for beginners: staff are trained in politeness, menus come with pictures, and everything follows a clear structure. The only missing ingredient is **the right vocabulary stash** — so your vacation's most anticipated moments don't turn into panic sessions.

This article collects the key phrases from entrance to checkout, plus an explanation of why Japanese menus feel like puzzles — and how to crack them.

## Why Japanese Restaurants Feel Different

A little context first, because it explains a lot. Japanese is spoken by roughly **123 million people**, nearly all within Japan itself — meaning English ability outside major cities varies wildly. Vocabulary prep isn't optional; it's essential.

The second factor is subtler but important: Japanese carries a **complex honorific system (*keigo*)** — special verb forms and vocabulary marking relative status of speaker and listener. Restaurant staff will greet you with high-register honorifics, and while customers aren't required to reply in full keigo, recognizing the patterns keeps your ears from shock. *Irasshaimase* is actually the honorific form of the verb *irassharu* — "to come/be present." You are being honored; no need to panic.

Third: Japanese is an ***agglutinative*** language with **subject-object-verb** order and particles marking grammatical function. The good news: in restaurant situations you barely need complex sentence structure. Short phrase + helper word = sufficient. Restaurants are Japan's most forgiving language gym.

## At the Door: Responding to Irasshaimase

The moment you step in, you'll hear *Irasshaimase!* or *Irasshai!* — "welcome." It's staff chatter, not a question, so you are **not obligated to answer**. A smile, a small nod, or a casual *"Konnichiwa"* is more than enough.

Seconds later staff usually appear to seat you, or ask how many. This is where numbers save you:

- **Hitori** (一人) — one person,
- **Futari** (二人) — two people,
- **San-nin** (三人) — three people,
- **Yonin** (四人) — four people.

Or deploy the ultimate tool: hold up fingers while smiling. Seriously — fingers + smile works in 99% of Japanese restaurants.

If you'd like to choose your table or mention a reservation: *Yoyaku shita ___ desu* ("I have a reservation under ___").

## Reading the Menu: Three Scripts and One Trap

Japanese menus can look intimidating thanks to a mix of three writing systems: **kanji** for main dish names, **hiragana** for grammatical bits, and **katakana** for foreign loanwords. Good news: katakana is your best friend at restaurants, because all foreign foods are written in it — ハンバーガー (*hanbāgā*, hamburger), ピザ (*piza*, pizza), サラダ (*sarada*, salad).

But beware a trap called ***wasei-eigo*** — "Japanese-made English": words with English roots whose meanings got modified. *Manshon* means an apartment, not a fancy mansion; and in the culinary world several terms wander off on their own. Never assume English sound = English meaning.

Some menu words worth memorizing:

- **Osusume** (おすすめ) — recommendation / special of the day,
- **Niku** (肉) — meat; **sakana** (魚) — fish; **yasai** (野菜) — vegetables,
- **Butaniku** — pork; **gyūniku** — beef; **toriniku** — chicken,
- **Mizu** (水) — water; **o-cha** (お茶) — tea; **bīru** (ビール) — beer,
- **Ōmori** (大盛り) — large portion; **shōmori** (小盛り) — small portion,
- **Dezāto** (デザート) — dessert.

Also notice the **o-** or **go-** prefixes before many words — honorific markers. *O-mizu* and *mizu* both mean water; the *o-* version sounds softer and is what staff typically use.

## Key Phrases for Ordering

Here's the core arsenal. Four sentences cover 90% of ordering situations:

**"Menyū o onegaishimasu."** (メニューをお願いします) — "Menu, please." The magic phrase ***onegaishimasu*** ("please") will serve you repeatedly all night. Here's the formula: **[desired item] + o + onegaishimasu**.

**"Kore o kudasai."** (これをください) — "This one, please." While pointing at a picture or text on the menu. ***Kudasai*** is the casual cousin of *onegaishimasu* — both correct, both welcomed by staff.

**"Osusume wa nan desu ka."** (おすすめは何ですか) — "What do you recommend?" A door-opening question: staff usually answer enthusiastically and sometimes walk straight to their favorite dish.

**"Eigo no menyū wa arimasu ka."** (英語のメニューはありますか) — "Is there an English menu?" There's zero shame in this question — plenty of tourist-friendly restaurants provide them.

For portion counts, use the counter ***ninmae*** (人前， "portions for ... people"): *"Ramen futari-mae o onegaishimasu"* — "two portions of ramen, please."

### Rescue Questions

A few extra phrases that regularly save the evening:

- **"Kore wa nan desu ka."** (これは何ですか) — "What is this?" — while pointing at the menu.
- **"___ ga arimasen."** — "We're out of ___ / none left" — staff language; treat the word *arimasen* as your alarm to pick something else.
- **"Sumimasen!"** (すみません) — Japan's number-one multipurpose word: "excuse me." Call staff, request help, apologize — one word does everything.
- **"O-kaikei onegaishimasu."** — save this one for later; we'll get there shortly.

## Restaurant Types, Vocabulary Types

Japanese restaurant vocabulary isn't one uniform package — each venue type carries its own rituals and word sets. Knowing them prepares you anywhere:

**Izakaya** — Japanese-style gastropub, paradise for small plates (*otsumami*) and drinks. Key words: *kanpai!* (raise glasses, "cheers!") and... beware ***otoshi***: a surprise mini-dish automatically served as a "seating charge" added to your bill. It's normal, not a scam. Order your first drink with *"Toriaezu bīru!"* ("beer to start") and you'll instantly sound local.

**Kaiten-zushi** (conveyor-belt sushi) — sushi plates glide past; take what you like and the cashier **counts the plates**. Useful vocabulary: *aburi* (partially seared), *agari* (in-house term for green tea), *gari* (pickled ginger palate cleanser). Pay by stating your plate-color count.

**Family restaurants** (famiresu) — 24-hour western-Japanese style diners. Drink bars (refillable), kids' menus, zero-pressure service. The safest haven for total beginners.

**Ramen shops** — often using door-side ticket machines (covered shortly), counter seating, fast ethics: eat while hot, slurping actually permitted.

**Depachika and food courts** — department-store basements selling premium side dishes; key words: *omochikaeri* (takeout) and *shōhinkibi* (today's expiry date — evening discounts!).


![Restaurant Vocabulary](/images/topics/bahasa-jepang-alt.svg)
*Image: Restaurant Vocabulary*

## Real Scenario: One Night at a Ramen Shop

Let's combine everything in a real scenario. You enter a tiny Tokyo ramen shop:

At the door sits a ticket machine. Its screen shows pictures: *Shōyu ramen* (880 yen), *Miso ramen* (920), *Tonkotsu* (900). Insert cash, press miso, plus the *chāshū aji-tamago* button (extra pork + egg). The machine dispenses two coupons. Take a counter seat and hand them over saying: *"Onegaishimasu."*

Minutes later staff asks briefly: *"Katame de daijōbu desu ka?"* — "firm noodles okay?" You recall noodle-firmness vocabulary: *yawarakame* (soft), *futsū* (regular), *katame* (firm). Answer: *"Hai, katame de!"*

The ramen arrives steaming. Quietly say *"Itadakimasu"*, then proceed: stir slightly, sip broth first, then devour. Mid-meal you want extra garlic — just raise a hand calling *"Sumimasen!"* and point at the table condiment: *"Kore o onegaishimasu."*

Finished. Lift your head from the bowl, tell staff *"Gochisōsama deshita"*, place the bowl on the return rack, and leave without paying again — everything was settled via coupons. The entire interaction needed five phrases. That's why restaurants are language training's best starting point: limited structure, predictable responses, mistakes still smiling.

## During the Meal: Words That Warm Hearts

Before your first bite, Japanese speakers say ***Itadakimasu*** — literally "I humbly receive (this life)." More than "bon appétit," it expresses gratitude toward the food and everyone who prepared it. Say it quietly, no drama needed — just say it.

While tasting, **"Oishii!"** (美味しい) — "delicious!" — is the most universal compliment and every chef's favorite. The more formal version, *oishikatta desu*, works well after finishing. Staff who catch an *oishii* paired with a smile know their work succeeded.

Mid-meal, when you need something: *Mizu o onegaishimasu* (water, please) or *O-hashi o onegaishimasu* (chopsticks, please). And when done, close with ***Gochisōsama deshita*** — "thank you for the feast." It's the official partner of *itadakimasu*, and saying it as you rise from your seat is a cultural touch that never fails to warm the room.

### Small Etiquette Worth Big Points

A few non-verbal moves that make staff adore you: never stick chopsticks vertically into rice (that's a funeral ritual); avoid shuffling plates from their original positions; and at many ramen shops, you order via a ticket machine at the entrance — show the coupon to staff without speaking a word.

On tipping: Japan has **no tipping culture**. Service charges are included, and leaving coins on the table may send staff chasing after you to return them. Your *gochisōsama* is their highest tip.

## Paying: The Simplest Moment of All

Final good news: paying in Japan is remarkably simple. In many casual restaurants you pay **at the register near the door** — not at the table. Just stand at the register and say:

**"O-kaikei onegaishimasu."** (お会計お願いします) — "The bill, please."

An equal alternative: *O-kanjō onegaishimasu*. Staff will present the receipt or tally the total, you pay — cash still rules at small restaurants, so keep bills and coins ready.

One final rescue phrase: **"Bunkatsu dekimasu ka?"** — "Can we split the bill?" — invaluable for group meals. And once the transaction closes, *Arigatō gozaimasu* ends the night perfectly.

Notice that *o-kaikei* and *o-kanjō* again carry the honorific prefix *o-* — consistent polite language from front door to exit is the very identity of Japanese service.

## Vocabulary for Difficult Situations

Now the advanced layer: phrases for non-ideal moments — precisely when language matters most.

**Allergies and dietary limits.** Rescue sentence: *"___ arerugī ga arimasu"* ("I'm allergic to ___") — fill with *ebi* (shrimp), *kani* (crab), *tamago* (egg), *gyūniku* (beef). For halal or vegetarian needs, longer phrasing helps: *"Niku wa tabemasen"* ("I don't eat meat"). In Japan, fish stock (*dashi*) often hides in seemingly vegetarian dishes — never hesitate to ask *"Dashi wa irimasu ka?"*

**Wrong orders arriving.** Point calmly and say *"Chigaimasu"* ("this is different") while showing the menu. Japanese staff are trained to apologize and replace quickly — no raised voices needed; calm is the most effective complaint language there.

**Requesting replacements.** The polite version of *"Mizu o kudasai"* is *"O-mizu o itadakemasu ka."* Too long? *Sumimasen* plus gestures still works. General principle: the more formal the sentence, the more respect conveyed — but short phrases are almost always welcomed with a smile.

**Lost ticket-machine coupons.** At ramen shops, show empty hands and say *"Kippu o nakushimashita"* ("I lost my ticket"). Staff typically help patiently — and here's a key lesson: honestly admitting mistakes in simple language always lands better than pretending nothing happened.

**Needing more ordering time.** Deploy universal honesty: *"Chotto matte kudasai"* ("please wait a moment") with a smile. No Japanese staff rushes customers.

Notice the common thread: in difficult situations, **simplicity + politeness + gestures** solve 95% of problems. You don't need speeches — just one right phrase delivered with the right attitude.

To close this section, one proven practice tip: **self role-play**. Before departure, run a full simulation in your head or with a friend — from entering the door to paying — using every phrase in this article. Say them aloud. Mouth automation matters as much as ear memorization: phrases spoken three times will emerge far more easily in real situations than phrases merely read ten times.

Finally, use technology as a safety net without letting it become a crutch. Save pictures of favorite menus, install an offline dictionary app, and learn your phone's camera-translation feature — useful for price tags or small notes at restaurants. But reach for them only when stuck: every transaction completed in your own words reduces screen dependence a little — and that is real progress.

But reach for them only when stuck: every transaction completed in your own words reduces screen dependence a little — and that is real progress.

As a bonus, notice how restaurant vocabulary transfers easily to other situations. The phrase *onegaishimasu* works in taxis, shops, and hotels; *sumimasen* applies almost everywhere; numbers and counters (*ninmae*, *hon*, *mai*) serve any shopping trip. Mastering one scenario thoroughly turns out to open many doors at once — which is why starting from restaurants is such a smart learning decision.

## Conclusion

Dining at Japanese restaurants turns out not to be a language exam but a learnable routine, masterable in one afternoon: greet *irasshaimase* with a smile, show numbers on your fingers, order with *kore o kudasai* and *onegaishimasu*, praise with *oishii*, close with *gochisōsama deshita*, and pay with *o-kaikei onegaishimasu*. Those ten phrases already make you more confident than 90% of tourists.

Better still, restaurants are Japan's finest language laboratory: structured situations, predictable responses, mistakes always forgiven with a smile. Every successful order without Google Translate raises your linguistic courage a level — and that level carries over to convenience stores, train stations, and the next conversation.

So drill those ten phrases before your flight. Then in Tokyo, when the whole room shouts *irasshaimase*, you won't freeze — you'll smile, sit down, and start ordering like someone who lives there.
